content: Cocoa butter, also known as theobroma oil, is a pale-yellow, pure, edible vegetable fat derived from cacao beans. It serves as the primary fat used in the production of solid chocolate bars. To create these bars, cocoa butter is combined with varying amounts of cocoa powder to form solid pieces of chocolate. This fat is extracted from cacao beans and is utilized not only in chocolate and cocoa powder production but also in pharmaceuticals, ointments, and toiletries. Cocoa butter is characterized by its mild chocolate flavor and aroma. During the processing of cacao beans, cocoa solids and cocoa butter are separated at an early stage. These components are later recombined during the manufacturing of regular (brown) chocolate bars. White chocolate, on the other hand, contains cocoa butter but does not include cocoa powder. Due to its melting temperature, cocoa butter is frequently used in pharmaceuticals as a base for suppositories. It can be stored at room temperature but melts readily at body temperature, allowing for the release of medication. Cocoa butter is one of the most stable fats known, containing natural antioxidants that prevent rancidity and provide a shelf life of two to five years. This stability makes it an excellent choice for non-food products. Its smooth texture, sweet fragrance, and emollient properties make it a popular ingredient in cosmetics and skincare products, such as soaps and lotions. The most common form of cocoa butter has a melting point of approximately 34 to 38 degrees Celsius (93 to 100 degrees Fahrenheit). This property allows chocolate to remain solid at room temperature while melting easily in the mouth. Cocoa butter exhibits polymorphism, forming α, γ, β', and β crystals, with melting points of 17, 23, 26, and 35–37 °C, respectively. Chocolate production typically utilizes only the β crystal form due to its higher melting point. A uniform crystal structure in cocoa butter results in a smooth texture, a glossy sheen, and a satisfying snap. However, overheating cocoa butter can alter its structure to a less stable form that melts below room temperature. Over time, it will naturally revert to the most stable β crystal form.
